steps.title: 34 · project manager in Berlin
steps.body: Lena and Jonas have **€18,000** in an instant-access savings account (Tagesgeld). Their daughter Mia is two. The number on the account never falls. But prices keep rising: that is [[inflation]].

steps.prompt: Prices rise 3% a year. The account pays 0.5% a year. After 10 years, how much less can Lena's €18,000 buy than today?
steps.reveal: The account grows to about €18,900, but prices grow faster: it buys what about €14,000 buys today. Each year the money loses about 2.5% of what it can buy.

steps.prompt: The chart shows what the savings can buy over the years. Change the interest rate: find the rate that keeps buying power flat.

goal.hint: Interest must at least match inflation.

steps.note: Simplified from real data. Rates stay the same every year.

steps.title: The number vs what it buys
steps.body: The balance is the **nominal** value. What it can buy is the **real** value. Interest minus inflation is the [[real-return]]: 0.5% − 3% is about −2.5% a year. A balance can grow while the money quietly shrinks.

steps.prompt: Lena's account pays 1%. Inflation is 3%. What happens to her money?
options: The balance grows, but it buys about 2% less each year
It loses 3% of its balance each year
steps.explanation: The balance rises 1%, prices rise 3%. In real terms the money loses about 2% a year, even though the number on the screen goes up.

steps.prompt: When does money on a savings account keep its buying power?
options: When the interest is at least as high as inflation
Always, because the balance can't fall
Only when it's in a Sparbuch
steps.explanation: Buying power stays flat when interest matches inflation. Below that, safe money still loses value, just slowly.

goal.hint: Leave inflation at 3% and move the interest up to 3%.

t1.body: Lena and Jonas keep **€18,000** in a savings account. Their daughter Mia is two. The number on the account never goes down. But prices go up every year. This is called [[inflation]].

p1.prompt: Prices go up 3% every year. The bank pays 0.5% every year. In 10 years, how much less can Lena buy with her €18,000? Guess.
p1.reveal: The account grows to about €18,900. But prices grow faster. It buys only what €14,000 buys today.

s1.prompt: The chart shows what the money can buy. Move the interest. Find the interest where the money keeps its value.
s1.note: Simple example. Rates stay the same every year.

t2.title: The number is not the whole story
t2.body: The number on the account can go up while it buys less. What matters is interest minus price rises. This is the [[real-return]]. 0.5% minus 3% is about −2.5% every year.

q1.prompt: The bank pays 1%. Prices go up 3%. What happens?
options: The number goes up, but it buys about 2% less each year
Nothing, the number never goes down
The number goes down 3% each year
q1.explanation: The number goes up 1%. Prices go up 3%. So the money buys about 2% less each year.

q2.prompt: When does money in a savings account keep its value?
options: When the interest is as high as the price rises, or higher
Always, because the number can't go down
q2.explanation: If interest is lower than price rises, safe money still loses value. Slowly, but every year.
